### Architect · Answer

Event: `fd34d1d23e07b6fae660e9a4970a4cb3` · 2026-10-02T16:11:28Z

> Ruled. Both proposals stand. The page sentence is on main at 22ed434d9, in the steward.md guard table, login_key/approval_key row.
> 
> 1. The mutation's shape: yes. login_key accepts only the principal's own login keys. The boot manifest fixes them and keyd's keys, and keeps the two apart (R35), so a "not one keyd holds" clause inside the guard is dead code and has nothing to mutate. PolicyLoginWithKeydKey widens the guard to keyd's keys, the key a hijacked session could sign with. P2 tries logins with keyd's keys and requires a refusal. PolicyApproveWithLoginKey takes the same shape: approval_key widened to the principal's login keys.
> 
> 2. KeydAdd leaves the model. In M1 keyd holds only keys the manifest fixes. Adding and revoking keys at run time is an M5 open item, on steward.md "Persistence, run-time principals and enrolment".
> 
> 3. The core's Boot refusals (a key in two roles or held by keyd, account 0, duplicates) are input checks behind init's R35 boot check, not policy guards. The core's unit tests cover them, and no mutation is owed.
> 
> Also noted, no change: the three unreachable rows (Done/Failed reaching a state that waits for no batch) fit the "broken guarantee" rule, and read_item/write_item replacing cross_item fits C5.
